text: This final lesson ties together every chapter of this course and the full Castellan-Thornbury merger Lessons 29 through 31 just ran end to end — identity, authentication, authorization, hardening, and governance, closing with what a graduate of this course is now specifically ready for.

Chapter 1's identity plane put Entra ID at the center as the surviving identity provider, with Okta federated in rather than ripped out on day one, and SAML and OIDC each driving their own migration path. Chapter 2's three-phase MFA rollout met Thornbury's SMS-based users exactly where they actually started. Chapter 3's authorization models are exactly where the gap behind the toxic combination traces back to.

Chapters 4 and 5's CIS-based Windows and Linux hardening closed real gaps across a previously unmanaged fleet, with a new GPO baseline and an Ansible playbook instead of manual, one-time fixes. Chapter 6's access certification campaign caught a toxic combination that had sat undetected for fourteen months. Chapter 7's controls-as-code discipline tested every hardening rule in audit mode first, and wrote the automated check that prevents the next one.

None of these five domains worked alone. The identity plane drove the MFA rollout. The role catalog's gap became a toxic combination only caught by governance. The hardening baseline was only safe to roll out because of controls-as-code testing — the same discipline that now prevents governance's own gap from recurring.

Deciding between federating and migrating two identity providers, designing a phased SSO and MFA rollout around two real starting points, building and safely deploying a CIS-based hardening baseline across mixed Windows and Linux fleets, and finding, sizing, and fixing a real toxic combination — that's the demonstrated toolkit of an IAM Engineer or a Security Engineer, not a certificate claim.

That's Security Engineering, IAM & System Hardening complete — seven chapters of identity, authentication, authorization, hardening, and governance, proven on one real merger. Course complete. Next up: Azure & AWS Cloud Security Engineering, continuing the Advanced Specialization stage.
